incidents.title: Unbounded in-memory queue
incidents.brief: Producers keep appending jobs in RAM while workers are stuck, and the process OOMs.
incidents.constraint: Work arrives faster than it completes.
incidents.question: What should producers see?

choices.label: Bound queue
choices.resultBody: A bounded queue that blocks, drops, or returns 429 when full instead of growing forever.

choices.label: Infinite buffer
choices.resultBody: An infinite buffer absorbs 4,000 jobs/s while workers are stuck, so memory climbs until the process is killed and every queued job in RAM is lost.

choices.label: Ignore lag
choices.resultBody: Ignoring worker lag lets the queue grow silently; by the time anyone looks, jobs are 50 minutes stale and the process runs out of memory anyway.

hints: Work arrives faster than it completes.
Unbounded buffers hide the fire.
Slow or reject producers.

incidents.title: Uploads say done, videos appear 6 hours later
incidents.brief: Clipstream's upload API returns 200 for every video. 7,200 uploads/min arrive, transcoders clear 5,000/min, and the queue holds 1.8 million jobs: a 6-hour wait users never see.
incidents.constraint: Transcode capacity is fixed until next quarter's GPU order.
incidents.question: What should the API tell uploaders once the backlog is too deep?

choices.label: Cap the queue and return 503 with Retry-After

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Honest, bounded wait; about 30% of peak uploads are deferred to off-peak.

choices.resultBody: The queue is capped at 150,000 jobs (~30 min of work); accepted uploads get 202 with a status URL, and the rest get 503 with Retry-After: 120, which the client retries with jitter. Cost: at peak ~30% of uploads are deferred, and clients must implement the retry.

choices.label: Autoscale the upload API to accept more videos
choices.resultBody: The API was never the bottleneck: with transcoders fixed at 5,000 jobs/min and 7,200 arriving, the queue still grows by 2,200 a minute and the wait passes 6.3 hours.

choices.label: Show a progress bar and hide queue depth
choices.resultBody: The bar stalls at 99%, users assume failure and upload again, and the duplicates push the backlog to 2.1 million jobs while tickets double to 260 an hour.

hints: The transcoders are doing their best; the promise at the front door is wrong.
An unbounded backlog turns a fast failure into a slow, invisible one.
HTTP status codes can carry a 'come back later' time.

incidents.title: Slow log collector freezes checkout
incidents.brief: Bazaarly's checkout logs through an async appender with a 10k-entry queue set to block when full. The log collector slowed to 200 lines/s against 4k lines/s produced, so request threads now wait inside log.info() and p95 hit 8 s.
incidents.constraint: Error and audit logs must never be lost.
incidents.question: What should happen when the log buffer is full?

choices.label: Discard DEBUG and INFO lines when the queue is 80% full

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Business traffic wins over diagnostics; low-level logs have gaps under pressure.

choices.resultBody: Past 80% full, the appender drops DEBUG and INFO and counts what it dropped, while WARN, ERROR and audit events still block to guarantee delivery. Threads stop waiting and p95 returns to 110 ms. Cost: during the slowdown, 70% of INFO lines are missing.

choices.label: Make the appender queue unbounded
choices.resultTitle: Heap fills, then the JVM dies
choices.resultBody: Threads stop blocking, but 3,800 unsent lines a second pile up in memory; after 25 minutes the heap passes 4 GB, GC pauses reach 6 s, and pods OOM, losing every buffered line including the errors.

choices.label: Log synchronously straight to the collector
choices.resultTitle: Every request now waits on the collector
choices.resultBody: Without a buffer, each log call is a network write to a collector that takes 200 ms to accept it; a checkout writes about 12 lines, so p95 rises to 12 s.

hints: Checkout isn't slow at checkout. It's slow at logging.
A full buffer can block, grow, or drop. Two of those hurt users.
Not every log line is worth a customer's wait.

incidents.title: Order-events consumer blows its heap every 12 minutes
incidents.brief: Shipwise's reactive consumer fetches 20,000 records/s from Kafka into memory, but its enrichment step can only do 500/s. The in-memory buffer passes 6 GB and the JVM OOMs every 12 minutes.
incidents.constraint: Enrichment calls a partner API hard-capped at 500 req/s across all consumers.
incidents.question: How should the consumer signal how much it can take?

choices.label: Pause partitions when in-flight records exceed 2,000

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Memory bounded; the backlog moves into Kafka as consumer lag.

choices.resultBody: The consumer calls pause() at 2,000 in-flight records and resume() below 500, still polling so it keeps its group membership; fetches match the 500/s partner cap and heap settles at 700 MB. Cost: the backlog now shows up as consumer lag, so topic retention must cover it and lag alerts replace OOM alerts.

choices.label: Raise the consumer heap from 8 GB to 32 GB
choices.resultBody: The buffer still grows by 19,500 records/s, so 32 GB only delays the crash, and multi-second full-GC pauses now trigger consumer-group rebalances on top.

choices.label: Add partitions and scale out to 40 consumer pods
choices.resultBody: 40 pods fetch in parallel, but the partner cap is still 500 req/s in total; each pod buffers its share, the partner starts returning 429s, and the pods' retries push errors to 900/s.

hints: Kafka is pull-based: who decides how much gets pulled?
The slow step's rate is fixed, so the buffer in front of it must be bounded.
The consumer API can stop fetching from partitions without leaving the group.

incidents.title: 2 million photos queued, autoscaler sees 35% CPU
incidents.brief: Snapfold's resize workers spend most of each job waiting on S3 reads and writes. A holiday surge sends 6k photos/s against 2k/s of capacity; the queue hits 2 million, but CPU stays at 35%, so the 70%-CPU autoscaler never adds workers.
incidents.constraint: Paying for peak capacity all year isn't an option.
incidents.question: What signal should drive scaling for these workers?

choices.label: Autoscale workers on the age of the oldest job

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Capacity tracks demand; brief lag while new workers start.

choices.resultBody: The scaler now targets an oldest-job age under 60 s; it grows the fleet from 40 to 130 workers in 6 minutes, drains the backlog in 25 minutes, and shrinks back overnight. Cost: queue metrics must be scraped every 15 s and S3 request costs rise during surges.

choices.label: Lower the CPU scaling target from 70% to 30%
choices.resultTitle: Scales, but not with the backlog
choices.resultBody: At 35% CPU the scaler adds some workers, but it stops once CPU averages 30%, long before the queue drains; at night the same target keeps 3x the needed workers running for nothing.

choices.label: Pin the fleet at 400 workers year-round
choices.resultBody: The queue drains in 8 minutes, but 400 workers idle at 5% CPU for 11 months of the year, adding about $38k a month, and a bigger surge than this one would still pile up.

hints: The workers are busy, just not busy on the CPU.
CPU is a proxy for load. Is it the right one here?
Scale on what users actually feel: how long jobs wait.

incidents.title: Payout workers get the API key banned
incidents.brief: Payfleet's bank partner allows 200 req/s and returns 429 with Retry-After: 2 above that. Payout workers retry 429s immediately in a loop, sending 6,000 req/s; the bank suspends the key for 15 minutes as a penalty.
incidents.constraint: The bank won't raise the 200 req/s quota this month.
incidents.question: How should the workers respond to the bank saying 'slow down'?

choices.label: Share a 180 req/s token bucket and obey Retry-After

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Stays within quota; backlog drains at a fixed pace.

choices.resultBody: All workers draw from one token bucket at 90% of quota and sleep for the Retry-After value on any 429; rejections fall to 0.2% and the 40k backlog clears in under 4 minutes. Cost: payouts beyond 180/s wait in the queue instead of trying.

choices.label: Add 30 more workers to push the backlog through
choices.resultBody: Sixty workers retrying in a loop send 12,000 req/s; the bank escalates the suspension to an hour, and the payout backlog grows to 90k.

choices.label: Sleep 100 ms before retrying each 429
choices.resultBody: Each of 30 workers now retries 10 times a second, so the bank still sees 3,000 req/s; most calls are rejected and the key is suspended again within 20 minutes.

hints: The bank is telling you exactly how long to wait.
30 workers each retrying on their own can't know the total rate.
Match the send rate to the quota before you hit it.

incidents.title: Search box fires a request per keystroke
incidents.brief: Booknook's search box fires a request per keystroke: 11 per search, 44k req/s at peak. The cluster sits at 95% CPU, and late responses overwrite newer ones, so 14% of users see results for 'harr' after typing 'harry potter'.
incidents.constraint: Results must still feel instant, under 300 ms after the user stops typing.
incidents.question: How do you cut the load the UI itself creates?

choices.label: Debounce 200 ms and abort the previous request

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Far less load and no out-of-order results; 200 ms of input delay.

choices.resultTitle: One request per pause in typing
choices.resultBody: The client waits for 200 ms without keystrokes before searching and aborts the in-flight call when a new one starts, so each search sends about 2 requests. Load falls to 8k req/s and stale results to 0. Cost: 200 ms of added delay before results appear.

choices.label: Cache every prefix query at the CDN for 5 minutes
choices.resultTitle: Popular prefixes cached, long tail isn't
choices.resultBody: Short prefixes like 'h' and 'ha' hit the cache, but most longer prefixes are unique, so the hit rate is 35%; the cluster still gets 29k req/s and stale out-of-order results remain.

choices.label: Add six nodes to the search cluster
choices.resultTitle: Twice the cost, same request storm
choices.resultBody: CPU falls to 55% and p95 to 300 ms, but the UI still sends 44k req/s, the cluster bill doubles, and late responses still overwrite newer ones for 9% of users.

hints: Most of these requests are for words the user hasn't finished.
A response to 'harr' is useless once the user types 'harry'.
Wait for a pause, and cancel what's already obsolete.

incidents.title: Workers serve requests nobody is waiting for
incidents.brief: During Tickety's presale, 12k req/s hit an API that serves 8k. A 5,000-deep request queue builds a 6 s wait, but clients time out at 2 s, so workers run at 100% on requests whose users already left.
incidents.constraint: Capacity can't grow before the presale ends in 40 minutes.
incidents.question: How do you get useful work out of the capacity you have?

choices.label: Drop queued requests older than the 2 s client timeout

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Capacity goes to live users; excess is rejected fast.

choices.resultTitle: Every processed request has a listener
choices.resultBody: Requests carry their arrival time; any that waited more than 1.5 s are rejected with 503 instead of processed, so workers spend all 8k req/s on live users. Useful responses rise from 3% to 66% of traffic. Cost: the other third get an immediate 'try again'.

choices.label: Double the request queue to 10,000 slots
choices.resultBody: The queue wait grows to 12 s, six times the client timeout; almost everything processed is for users who left long ago, and memory per pod rises by 900 MB.

choices.label: Raise the client timeout to 10 s
choices.resultTitle: Users wait 6 s, then refresh anyway
choices.resultBody: Some requests now complete, but fans staring at a 6 s spinner hit refresh, adding duplicate requests; traffic rises to 15k req/s and the queue wait climbs to 9 s.

hints: The servers are fully busy, yet almost nobody gets an answer.
Compare the queue wait with how long the client is willing to wait.
Work that finishes after the client left is wasted capacity.

incidents.title: Replaying a 3-day backlog knocks out the points API
incidents.brief: Loyalto's points consumers were down for 3 days, and Kafka kept 26 million events. On restart the autoscaler launched 200 consumers, which write 40k rows/s into a Postgres rated for 5k. The live points API on that DB now times out.
incidents.constraint: No events may be skipped; every customer must get their points.
incidents.question: How fast should the backlog be replayed?

choices.label: Throttle replay to 3k DB writes a second

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Live traffic protected; backlog completes in hours, not minutes.

choices.resultTitle: Backlog drains while the API lives
choices.resultBody: Consumers share a 3k writes/s limit, leaving 2k/s of headroom for live traffic; the points API recovers to 60 ms and the 26M backlog drains in about 2.5 hours. Cost: some customers see their points show up hours late.

choices.label: Point the points API at a new read replica
choices.resultTitle: Reads move, but lag by hours
choices.resultBody: API reads stop timing out, but the replica can't replay 40k writes/s either; it falls 3 hours behind, balances look wrong to customers, and the primary stays at 100% CPU.

choices.label: Reset consumer offsets to the latest event
choices.resultBody: Load drops instantly, but 3 days of purchases never earn points; support gets 18,000 tickets in a day and finance must reconstruct balances from order history.

hints: The consumers are healthy and fast. That's the problem.
Kafka can deliver far faster than the database can absorb.
Let the slowest component set the replay pace.

incidents.title: gRPC stream server fills its heap with unsent frames
incidents.brief: Tracefeed streams 40 MB/s of telemetry per client over gRPC. Slow mobile dashboards drain 2 MB/s, yet the server keeps calling onNext(), and 3 GB of queued frames pile up in memory.
incidents.constraint: HTTP/2 already enforces per-stream flow-control windows between client and server.
incidents.question: How should the server react to a slow reader?

choices.label: Send only when isReady(), resume in the onReady handler

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Memory bounded by the window; slow clients must receive sampled data.

choices.resultBody: The server checks isReady() before each onNext() and parks the stream until the onReady handler fires, so writes follow the client's HTTP/2 window and queued frames drop to 40 MB. Cost: a 2 MB/s client can't get 40 MB/s, so the server now samples or drops stale telemetry for slow streams.

choices.label: Raise the HTTP/2 stream window to 64 MB
choices.resultBody: A larger window lets the server push more before blocking, but the phone still reads 2 MB/s; buffers swell on both ends and delay grows to 60 s.

choices.label: Spill each stream's pending frames to local disk
choices.resultBody: The heap OOM turns into ~130 GB/hour of disk writes; dashboards fall 10 minutes behind live data and the volume fills before the evening peak.

hints: The protocol is already saying 'slow down'; the application isn't listening.
Flow-control windows only help if the sender waits when they close.
Look at the stream observer's readiness signal.

incidents.title: Checkout times out behind bulk CSV exports
incidents.brief: At 11:00 Tallybook's API receives 14,000 req/s against 9,000 req/s of capacity. Checkout, bulk CSV exports and health checks share one queue, and every class times out after 30 s.
incidents.constraint: Checkout revenue must be protected; exports can wait several minutes.
incidents.question: Which requests should fail first, and where?

choices.label: Shed exports first via priority admission at the gateway

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Critical traffic protected; low-priority work is deferred and the priority map needs upkeep.

choices.resultBody: The gateway tags requests critical, default or sheddable; above the concurrency limit it rejects exports with 503 + Retry-After before they use any API capacity, and checkout p95 returns to 180 ms. Cost: exports stall for ~20 minutes at peak, and the priority map must be kept current as endpoints change.

choices.label: Lower every request timeout from 30 s to 5 s
choices.resultBody: Requests now die at 5 s instead of 30 s, but checkout still waits in the same queue behind exports, so about a third of checkouts keep timing out.

choices.label: Randomly drop 35% of requests at the load balancer
choices.resultBody: Random drop brings load under 9,000 req/s, but it rejects checkouts as readily as exports: 35% of paying shoppers are turned away while exports keep their share.

hints: Not all 14,000 requests are worth the same.
Shedding is cheapest before a request consumes any capacity.
Classify at the edge and reject the class you can most afford to lose.

incidents.title: One dashboard load fires 400 RPCs at once
incidents.brief: Metricly's dashboard page fetches each of its 400 widgets with a separate RPC, all fired in parallel. At 2k dashboard loads/s that is 800k RPCs/s in bursts; sidecar queues overflow and 21% of dashboards fail.
incidents.constraint: The widget service can't be merged into the dashboard service.
incidents.question: How do you keep one request from flooding the mesh?

choices.label: Batch into 8 multi-get calls, at most 4 in flight

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Bounded fan-out; coarser failure units per batch.

choices.resultBody: Widgets are fetched 50 per call through a batch endpoint, with a per-request semaphore of 4, so each dashboard sends 8 RPCs instead of 400. Mesh load falls to 16k RPCs/s and p95 to 450 ms. Cost: one slow batch delays 50 widgets, not one.

choices.label: Raise the sidecar pending-request limit to 10,000
choices.resultBody: Sidecars stop rejecting, so full 800k RPC/s bursts land on the widget service, which runs out of CPU and pushes dashboard p95 to 9 s with 30% errors.

choices.label: Cache each widget response for 10 s
choices.resultBody: Popular shared widgets hit the cache, but most analysts have personal filters, so the hit rate is 30%; each dashboard still fires 280 parallel calls and errors only fall to 12%.

hints: Count the calls behind one page view.
Nothing limits how many calls a single request can have in flight.
Fewer, bigger calls, with a cap on how many run at once.

incidents.title: 300k phones upload their whole backlog at once
incidents.brief: Fitloop's sync API was down for 2 hours. When it returned, 300k phones reconnected within a minute, each posting its full backlog, about 5,000 events in one 40 MB request. Sync pods OOM within seconds and phones retry.
incidents.constraint: Old app versions stay in use; the fix must ship in the next app release and on the server.
incidents.question: How should phones send a big backlog without overwhelming the server?

choices.label: Upload in 500-event pages, one page in flight per device

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Bounded memory per device; large backlogs arrive gradually.

choices.resultTitle: Backlogs trickle in page by page
choices.resultBody: Each phone sends a 4 MB page and waits for the ack before the next, and the server answers 503 with Retry-After when busy; memory per request drops 10x and the whole backlog lands in about 20 minutes. Cost: a phone with a week of data takes a few minutes to catch up.

choices.label: Raise the body limit and heap to fit 100 MB uploads
choices.resultBody: Pods now hold more 40 MB bodies at once before they die, so each OOM takes out more in-flight syncs; 300k phones retrying whole backlogs keep failures at 80%.

choices.label: Add a random 0-10 minute delay before reconnecting
choices.resultBody: Reconnects spread over 10 minutes, but each phone still posts one 40 MB body; 500 concurrent uploads need 20 GB of buffers, so pods still OOM, just less often, and 35% of syncs fail.

hints: The problem is how big each request is, not only how many there are.
A phone offline for a week sends a week of data in one go.
Let the client send a little, wait for the server, then send more.

incidents.title: Rejected uploads still crash the server
incidents.brief: Docuvault's upload service rejects work when its 50-task executor is full, but the HTTP layer first reads each 20 MB body into memory. At 400 concurrent uploads that is 8 GB buffered just to send 503, and pods OOM hourly.
incidents.constraint: Uploads can't go straight to object storage from the client this quarter.
incidents.question: Where should the service say 'no'?

choices.label: Check capacity on headers and reject before reading the body

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Memory bounded by admitted work; rejected uploads are retried by clients.

choices.resultTitle: 503 costs a few bytes, not 20 MB
choices.resultBody: The service now takes an executor permit when headers arrive and answers 503 with Retry-After, before reading the body, if none is free; clients using Expect: 100-continue never send it at all. Heap falls to 45% and OOMs stop. Cost: rejected clients must retry the whole upload.

choices.label: Raise the heap from 8 GB to 32 GB
choices.resultBody: More heap holds more buffered rejections before it fills, and full GCs on 32 GB now pause for 9 s, timing out uploads that were actually accepted.

choices.label: Give the executor a 5,000-task waiting queue
choices.resultBody: Uploads now wait in the queue with their 20 MB bodies already in memory; 2,000 queued bodies need 40 GB, so pods OOM in 15 minutes instead of an hour.

hints: The executor is protecting itself. Something upstream isn't.
Rejecting a request still costs whatever you've already read.
Decide before the expensive part arrives.

incidents.title: Hedged requests triple load on a slow origin
incidents.brief: Newsdash's mobile SDK re-sends any request unanswered after 300 ms, and again at 600 ms. At peak the feed API slows to 800 ms, so every request becomes three: 30k req/s of users turn into 90k at the origin.
incidents.constraint: Normal p95 is 180 ms, and tail latency matters to the feed team.
incidents.question: How do you keep hedging's tail-latency benefit without it multiplying load?

choices.label: Cap hedges at 5% of calls, sent only after p95

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Tail-latency benefit kept; hedging backs off exactly when load is high.

choices.resultTitle: Hedges help the tail, not the herd
choices.resultBody: The SDK now waits for the observed p95 before hedging, sends at most one extra copy, and stops hedging once hedges exceed 5% of its recent calls. When the origin slows, hedging switches itself off; load falls to 31k req/s and p95 to 200 ms. Cost: slightly slower tails under load.

choices.label: Lower the hedge delay to 100 ms
choices.resultBody: Now almost every request is hedged, even on a healthy origin; load rises to 110k req/s, the feed API falls further behind, and timeouts climb to 29%.

choices.label: Scale the feed API to three times its current nodes
choices.resultTitle: Pays for the copies, until the next slowdown
choices.resultBody: With three times the nodes the origin absorbs 90k req/s and p95 falls to 250 ms, but two-thirds of the fleet serves duplicates, the bill triples, and any slowdown past 300 ms triples load again.

hints: Users didn't triple. Copies did.
Hedges fire more exactly when the origin is slowest.
Hedging needs a budget that shrinks as the origin struggles.

incidents.title: Fixed rate limit lets a slow database melt the API
incidents.brief: Parcelly's gateway admits a fixed 8,000 req/s. When a Postgres vacuum raises query time from 5 ms to 40 ms, the same 8,000 req/s means 320 in-flight requests instead of 40, and p95 hits 9 s.
incidents.constraint: Database latency swings every hour; no single fixed limit suits both 5 ms and 40 ms.
incidents.question: What limit adapts to how fast the backend is actually draining?

choices.label: Adaptive concurrency limit driven by measured latency

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Tracks real capacity; throughput drops during slow periods and the limiter needs tuning.

choices.resultBody: The gateway compares live latency to its no-load baseline and cuts the concurrency cap multiplicatively when it rises, growing it additively when it falls; in-flight settles near 60, excess gets fast 503s, and p95 drops to 150 ms. Cost: throughput falls to ~1,500 req/s while vacuum runs, and the limiter needs tuning to avoid oscillation.

choices.label: Lower the fixed rate limit to 4,000 req/s
choices.resultBody: At 40 ms, 4,000 req/s is still 160 in flight and p95 stays near 4 s; once the vacuum ends, the limit rejects half the traffic a 5 ms database could have served.

choices.label: Retry timed-out requests twice with exponential backoff
choices.resultBody: Each timeout now costs up to three attempts, pushing effective load toward 14,000 req/s; in-flight passes 500 and API pods start OOM-restarting.

hints: The request rate didn't change; something else multiplied the in-flight work.
In-flight = rate x latency, and latency is the variable here.
Let the limit move with a latency signal instead of a constant.
